summary: I designed and empirically tested the geospatial core for route-buffer shop discovery directly against the live truckintel-pg database (PostgreSQL 16.4 / PostGIS 3.4.3), using real data: 109,777 Delaware OSM ways, 108,056 national OSM fuel stations, 629,710 national NBI bridges, 2,981 NYC businesses. Because there is no routes table, I built one (schema lane6) with two REAL routes assembled from osm.ways — I-95 Delaware NB/SB carriageways (35 km, 96 m vertex spacing) and US-13 Delaware (425 km, 4,210 vertices, 101 m spacing) — plus two clearly-labelled SYNTHETIC long-haul corridors for national-scale stress. On segmentation: ST_Segmentize is a densifier, not a splitter (367 pts in, 374 out, one geometry); ST_DumpSegments produces wildly non-uniform work units (min 1.4 m, max 7,880 m, sd 414.9 m); naive equal-fraction ST_LineSubstring drifts up to +16.4% because the fraction is measured in planar DEGREES; my measured-fraction chunker (lane6.route_chunks) hits ±0.8% with provably zero fraction gaps, zero geometry gaps, frac 0→1, and covered length bit-equal to route length. I found and reproduced a hard bug: ST_LineSubstring(geography,...) in PostGIS 3.4.3 silently TRUNCATES multi-vertex lines — a 3-vertex meridian line of 55,510.1 m returns 41,632.6 m at fractions (0,1) — so the geography variant must never be used. On buffering, the winner is a functional GIST index on (geom::geography) plus plain ST_DWithin(geography): 18.0 ms warm vs 4,321 ms without the index (240×), and it is latitude-correct, whereas the popular fixed-degree ST_Expand bbox prefilter is a silent false-negative generator (I constructed a shop at exactly 4,000 m at 64.5°N that fails `&& ST_Expand(route, 0.06)` while genuinely being within 5 km). Chunking is the single biggest win at scale: on the real 425 km route, 5 km chunks cut the fuel-station query from 305 ms to 34 ms (9.0×) and the bridges query from 1,022 ms to 99 ms (10.3×) with byte-identical results (169/169, 561/561) at every chunk size from 1 to 50 km. For nearest-point, ST_ClosestPoint(geometry) on EPSG:4326 is materially wrong — max 163.3 m / avg 20.8 m distance error and up to 1,637 m positional offset on 169 real rows — while ST_ClosestPoint(geography,...,true) is exact (0.000 m error vs ST_Distance) and costs the same (88.0 ms vs 79.2 ms), so there is no reason ever to use the planar variant. The full one-pass enrichment (nearest point + distance + fraction-along + heading + side-of-travel) runs in 87 ms for a 425 km route with 169 shops — the trig is effectively free next to the buffer scan. Travel-direction/side-of-carriageway via ST_Azimuth + sine-of-bearing-difference validated at 91.3% (42 of 46 shops that matched BOTH real I-95 carriageways flipped side correctly; 3 of the 4 failures sat within 135 m of both carriageways, i.e. in the median). Junction nodes are NOT ingestible today: scripts/osm_ways_job.py applies `EntityFilter(osmium.osm.WAY)`, so highway=motorway_junction nodes are discarded — zero exist in the DB, and motorway_link ways are no substitute (650 links, only 36 with a ref, 0 with a name). Finally, two operational landmines: every spatial table had n_live_tup=0, meaning ANALYZE had never been run (I ran it), and the server is on stock config — shared_buffers 128 MB, work_mem 4 MB, random_page_cost 4 on SSD — which alone caused a 2,981-row dedup self-join to take 10.9 s until I added the geography index (555 ms, 19.7× faster).

sources.name: PostGIS ST_LineSubstring documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Documents the geography variant added in 3.4.0 and states 'Geography implementation measures along a spheroid, geometry along a line'. I VERIFIED ON THE LIVE DB that this is broken in 3.4.3: ST_LineSubstring('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography,0,1) returns 41,632.6 m of a true 55,510.1 m line, output WKT truncated at lat 39.375. Do not use it.
sources.caveats: I searched trac.osgeo.org and found no matching ticket; treat the upstream-bug status as [UNVERIFIED] while the local reproducer is verified.

sources.name: PostGIS ST_ClosestPoint documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Confirms the geography signature ST_ClosestPoint(geography, geography, use_spheroid boolean). My measurements show this variant is exact (0.000 m error vs ST_Distance on 169 real rows) while the geometry variant on 4326 is off by up to 163.3 m — and both cost the same.

sources.name: PostGIS ST_DWithin documentation
sources.why_it_matters: The geography form is the correct 'within N metres' test for US data. EXPLAIN shows PostGIS rewrites it to `(geom)::geography && _ST_Expand((route)::geography, 5000)` — PostGIS computes the latitude-correct degree expansion itself, which is exactly why hand-rolled fixed-degree ST_Expand prefilters are unsafe.

sources.name: PostGIS ST_Azimuth documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Basis of the side-of-carriageway derivation. Azimuth is clockwise from north, so sin(bearing_to_shop - route_heading) > 0 means the shop is on the driver's RIGHT. Validated at 91.3% on the two real I-95 Delaware carriageways.

sources.name: PostGIS ST_DumpSegments documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Evaluated as a segmentation candidate and REJECTED: on the real I-95 DE route it emits 366 segments with min 1.4 m / avg 95.8 m / max 7,880 m / sd 414.9 m. Segment size is dictated by source vertices, so it cannot be used as a work unit.

sources.name: PostGIS ST_Segmentize documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Commonly mistaken for a splitter. Verified: one geometry in, ONE geometry out (367 -> 374 vertices). Its real value here is as a PRE-STEP — ST_Segmentize(route::geography, 1000) before chunking a vertex-sparse route (I measured a 4-vertex, 428 km route densify to 577 vertices).

sources.name: PostGIS ST_LineLocatePoint documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Provides fraction-along-line. Unlike ST_LineSubstring, the geography variant IS trustworthy — I tested a point at the exact 25% mark of a 3-vertex meridian line: geometry returned 0.250000, geography returned 0.249992.

sources.name: PostGIS KNN / geometry_distance_knn documentation
sources.why_it_matters: The <-> operator. I proved index-assisted KNN works against the functional geography index (EXPLAIN shows `Index Scan ... Order By: ((geom)::geography <-> ...)`) at 0.405 ms per probe on 108,056 rows. Caveat measured: geography <-> returns a sphere approximation (75.209) vs exact ST_Distance (75.203), so use <-> only for ORDERING, never for the published distance value.

sources.name: PostgreSQL 16 expression-index documentation
sources.why_it_matters: Basis for `CREATE INDEX ... USING GIST ((geom::geography))`. The expression in the query must match the index expression textually for the planner to use it — this is the single highest-leverage change in this whole lane (240x on fuel_stations, 19.7x on the dedup self-join).

sources.name: OSM wiki: highway=motorway_junction
sources.why_it_matters: The ONLY free legal national source for exit numbers (ref) and junction names. It is a NODE tag, and the repo's osmium pass discards nodes entirely, so this field is currently unfillable — see unfillable_or_risky.

sources.name: Open Database License (ODbL) 1.0
sources.why_it_matters: Governs everything in the osm.* schema. The repo's ruling §3.1-4a (OSM lives only in osm.*, joined at query time) plus core.businesses CHECK (present_in <@ ARRAY['overture','fsq']) is the share-alike firewall. My route_shops design deliberately stores only a REFERENCE plus derived geometry facts, never copied OSM attribute values — but see unfillable_or_risky: routes derived FROM osm.ways are themselves ODbL-derived.

sources.name: trac.osgeo.org/postgis (bug tracker)
sources.why_it_matters: Where the ST_LineSubstring(geography) truncation should be reported. Reachable (200) but I did NOT find an existing matching ticket via web search — the upstream status is [UNVERIFIED].

recommendations: SEGMENTATION — use generate_series + ST_LineSubstring on GEODESICALLY-MEASURED fractions. I built and tested lane6.route_chunks(route geometry(LineString,4326), chunk_m). It dumps vertices, accumulates BOTH planar-degree and geography-metre cumulative length per vertex, then linearly interpolates each metre boundary back into a planar fraction (because ST_LineSubstring's fraction is planar). Result on the real 425 km US-13 route at 2 km: min=max=2000 m, sd=0.0, sum=35047.6 m == route length 35047.6 m exactly. Gap proof (run it): SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE nxt_start IS NOT NULL AND frac_end <> nxt_start) AS fraction_gaps, count(*) FILTER (WHERE nxt_sp IS NOT NULL AND NOT ST_Equals(ep, nxt_sp)) AS geometry_gaps FROM (SELECT frac_end, lead(frac_start) OVER (ORDER BY seq) nxt_start, ST_EndPoint(geom) ep, lead(ST_StartPoint(geom)) OVER (ORDER BY seq) nxt_sp FROM lane6.route_chunks(<route>, 5000)) p; -> 0 and 0, first_frac=0, last_frac=1. Full function source is in the live DB: docker exec truckintel-pg psql -U truckintel -d truckintel -c "\\sf lane6.route_chunks".

SEGMENTATION — the three rejected alternatives, with the measurement that rejected each. (a) ST_Segmentize is a DENSIFIER not a splitter: ST_GeometryType(ST_Segmentize(geom::geography,1000)::geometry)='ST_LineString', npts 367->374, one row out. (b) ST_DumpSegments gives one row per vertex pair — 366 segments on I-95 DE with min 1.4 m / avg 95.8 m / max 7,880 m / sd 414.9 m; segment size is a property of the source data, so it is useless as a scheduling unit. (c) Naive equal-fraction ST_LineSubstring(geom, i/n, (i+1)/n) drifts because the fraction is in DEGREES: on a 4,689 km route with a 25,000 m target it produced 23,472..29,089 m (sd 1,601, +16.4% worst case); on I-95 DE with a 2,000 m target, 1,793..2,123 m (-10.3%/+6.2%).

SEGMENTATION — NEVER use ST_LineSubstring(geography, ...) on PostGIS 3.4.3. It silently truncates multi-vertex lines. Airtight reproducer, run it yourself: SELECT postgis_lib_version(), ST_Length('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography) AS truth, ST_Length(ST_LineSubstring('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography,0,1)) AS substring_0_1, ST_AsText(ST_LineSubstring('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography,0,1)::geometry); -> 3.4.3 | 55510.128 | 41632.596 | LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75.00000000000001 39.37500403715597). It stops at exactly 75% of the line. On the 22-vertex synthetic transcontinental route it returned 1,633,673 m of a 4,688,908 m line (34.8%) and 9 of 22 vertices. The geometry variant round-trips correctly (22/22 vertices). Add a startup assertion so a future PostGIS upgrade cannot silently reintroduce this.

SEGMENTATION — densify vertex-sparse routes BEFORE chunking. Chunk cut points are computed in planar degrees, so on a route whose vertices are far apart the chunked polyline is not the same locus as the geodesic reading of the parent line. Measured: on the synthetic 4,689 km route (223 km average vertex spacing) whole-route found 11,298 bridges but chunked found 11,364 (+66, 0.58% divergence). On REAL routed geometry it is bit-exact lossless: I-95 DE (96 m spacing) gave 123 == 123 fuel stations and 393 == 393 bridges; US-13 DE (101 m spacing) gave 169 and 561 identically at chunk sizes 1, 2, 5, 10, 25 and 50 km. Rule: if length_m / (ST_NPoints(geom)-1) > 200 then route := ST_Segmentize(route::geography, 1000)::geometry(LineString,4326) first (a 4-vertex 428 km route densified to 577 vertices in ~1.4 s).

BUFFER — the correct AND fast pattern is a functional GIST index on the geography cast plus plain ST_DWithin(geography). CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY <t>_geog_gix ON <schema>.<table> USING GIST ((geom::geography)); then WHERE ST_DWithin(f.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 5000). Measured on osm.fuel_stations (108,056 rows), same 123-row answer every time: no index -> Parallel Seq Scan, 4,321 ms. Functional geography index -> Index Scan, 68 ms cold / 18.05 ms warm (240x). PostGIS rewrites the predicate to `(geom)::geography && _ST_Expand((s.geom)::geography, '5000')` — it computes the latitude-correct degree expansion itself, which is the whole point.

BUFFER — do NOT hand-roll a fixed-degree bbox prefilter. `f.geom && ST_Expand(r.geom, 0.06) AND ST_DWithin(f.geom::geography, r.geom::geography, 5000)` benchmarks fine (15.5 ms) and is a silent false-negative generator. Constructed proof, verified: WITH route AS (SELECT ST_GeomFromText('LINESTRING(-147.7 64.0,-147.7 65.0)',4326) g), shop AS (SELECT ST_Project(ST_SetSRID(ST_MakePoint(-147.7,64.5),4326)::geography, 4000, radians(90))::geometry g) SELECT ST_Distance(shop.g::geography, route.g::geography), shop.g && ST_Expand(route.g,0.06), ST_DWithin(shop.g::geography, route.g::geography, 5000) FROM route, shop; -> 4000.0 m | f | t. A shop at exactly 4 km is dropped by the bbox at 64.5N. If you must hand-roll it, use the two-argument form ST_Expand(geom, dx, dy) with dx = buffer_m/(111320*cos(radians(max_abs_lat))) and dy = buffer_m/110574 — but the functional geography index makes this unnecessary.

BUFFER — ST_Buffer is the wrong tool. ST_Intersects(f.geom, ST_Buffer(r.geom::geography, 5000)::geometry) returned the identical 123 rows in 952 ms — 53x slower than the indexed ST_DWithin (18 ms) — because PostGIS internally runs _ST_BestSRID + ST_Transform + ST_Buffer + ST_Transform back for every evaluation (visible verbatim in the EXPLAIN Index Cond). Only materialize a buffer polygon if you need the polygon itself as an output artifact.

BUFFER — geography(spheroid) is the reference; know the error of every alternative. Measured on the 123 real fuel stations inside a 5 km band of I-95 DE, against ST_Distance(geography, spheroid=true): geography with use_spheroid=false (sphere) max 11.244 m / 0.245%; EPSG:32618 UTM 18N max 1.78 m / 0.040%; EPSG:5070 NAD83 CONUS Albers max 45.01 m / 0.934%. EPSG:5070 is EQUAL-AREA — never use it for distance. If you ever need planar speed, use the per-route UTM zone, not 5070. For this platform, just use geography: it is exact and already fast enough.

CHUNKING PAYOFF — this is the single biggest performance lever, quantified. Real dense 425 km US-13 route, 5 km buffer, warm cache, identical results at every size. vs osm.fuel_stations (108,056): whole route 305 ms; 1 km/426 segs 76 ms; 2 km/213 segs 56 ms; 5 km/86 segs 34 ms (BEST, 9.0x); 10 km 39 ms; 25 km 50 ms; 50 km 59 ms. vs core.bridges (629,710): whole route 1,022 ms; 1 km 224 ms; 2 km 141 ms; 5 km 99 ms (BEST, 10.3x); 10 km 176 ms; 25 km 139 ms; 50 km 179 ms. All 12 runs returned exactly 169 and 561. On the sparse synthetic 4,689 km route the optimum shifts to 25-100 km (bridges: whole 16,889 ms -> 50 km 168 ms). RECOMMENDATION: 5 km chunks for real routed geometry; that is also the natural buffer-radius scale so per-chunk false positives drop from 93% (whole route) to ~47%.

NEAREST POINT — one-pass SQL that yields (nearest_point_geom, distance_m, fraction_along_route) plus m_along and heading, measured at 87 ms for a 425 km route / 169 shops. The trig is free relative to the buffer scan (79 ms for the buffer alone). Pattern: WITH cand AS (SELECT s.route_id, s.seq, s.m_start, s.len_m, s.geom seg_geom, f.osm_id, f.geom shop_geom FROM route_segments s JOIN LATERAL (SELECT osm_id, geom FROM osm.fuel_stations f WHERE ST_DWithin(f.geom::geography, s.geom::geography, 5000)) f ON TRUE WHERE s.route_id=$1), best AS (SELECT DISTINCT ON (osm_id) * FROM cand ORDER BY osm_id, ST_Distance(shop_geom::geography, seg_geom::geography)) SELECT b.osm_id, np.g::geometry AS nearest_point_geom, ST_Distance(b.shop_geom::geography, np.g) AS distance_m, b.m_start + lf.f*b.len_m AS m_along_route, (b.m_start + lf.f*b.len_m)/rt.length_m AS fraction_along_route, degrees(az.a) AS route_heading_deg, CASE WHEN az.a IS NULL THEN NULL WHEN sin(ST_Azimuth(np.g::geometry, b.shop_geom) - az.a) > 0 THEN 'right' ELSE 'left' END AS side_of_travel FROM best b JOIN routes rt ON rt.route_id=b.route_id, LATERAL (SELECT ST_LineLocatePoint(b.seg_geom::geography, b.shop_geom::geography, true) f) lf, LATERAL (SELECT ST_ClosestPoint(b.seg_geom::geography, b.shop_geom::geography, true) g) np, LATERAL (SELECT ST_Azimuth(ST_LineInterpolatePoint(b.seg_geom, greatest(lf.f-0.002,0)), ST_LineInterpolatePoint(b.seg_geom, least(lf.f+0.002,1))) a) az;

NEAREST POINT — use ST_ClosestPoint(geography, geography, true), never the geometry variant on 4326. Measured on 169 real shops at 5 km segment level: the planar closest point gives max 163.315 m / avg 20.772 m DISTANCE error, and sits up to 1,637.10 m / avg 189.28 m away ALONG THE LINE from the true geodesic foot. Worst real case: osm_id way/305804177, true 2,585.9 m vs planar 2,684.4 m, planar foot at POINT(-75.51823 39.14294) vs geodesic foot at POINT(-75.52899 39.13081). Cause: in EPSG:4326 planar space a longitude degree is only 0.777x a latitude degree in ground metres at 39N, so the planar perpendicular is not the ground perpendicular. The geography variant is EXACT (max |ST_Distance(shop, closest_point) - ST_Distance(shop, line)| = 0.000 m) and costs the same: 88.0 ms vs 79.2 ms for the whole query.

NEAREST POINT — useful identity, verified: ST_LineInterpolatePoint(g, ST_LineLocatePoint(g, pt)) is geometrically IDENTICAL to ST_ClosestPoint(g, pt) — max separation 0.000000 m over 169 real rows (ST_Equals reported 141/169 only because of float-bit representation, so compare with ST_Distance, not ST_Equals). Both are planar and therefore both carry the 163 m error above. Convert m_along as m_start + fraction * segment_len_m using the GEOGRAPHY fraction from ST_LineLocatePoint(seg::geography, shop::geography, true) — inside a 5 km segment that product is exact by construction, and it avoids paying for ST_Length(ST_LineSubstring(...)) per shop.

NEAREST — KNN <-> is for ORDERING only, never for the published distance. Index-assisted KNN works against the functional geography index: EXPLAIN shows `Index Scan using lane6_fuel_geog_gix ... Order By: ((geom)::geography <-> ...)` at 0.405 ms per probe over 108,056 rows (86 probes in 45 ms). But geography <-> returns a sphere approximation: 75.209 vs true ST_Distance 75.203, 366.733 vs 366.688. Use LATERAL (... ORDER BY col::geography <-> $pt::geography LIMIT k) to get candidates, then recompute the published distance with ST_Distance(geography). Note the KNN index path needs the probe geometry to be a per-row constant, i.e. it only kicks in inside a LATERAL — a plain two-table ORDER BY <-> will seq-scan.

TRAVEL DIRECTION — ST_Azimuth + sine of bearing difference works and I validated it on real divided-highway data. side = CASE WHEN sin(ST_Azimuth(nearest_point, shop_point) - route_heading) > 0 THEN 'right' ELSE 'left' END, where route_heading = ST_Azimuth(ST_LineInterpolatePoint(seg, f-0.002), ST_LineInterpolatePoint(seg, f+0.002)) clamped to [0,1]. Azimuth is clockwise from north, so a positive sine means the shop is to the driver's right. Validation: 46 shops matched BOTH real I-95 Delaware carriageways (NB headings 36-90 deg, SB headings 217-272 deg, correctly opposite). 42 of 46 (91.3%) flipped side correctly between carriageways.

TRAVEL DIRECTION — set side_of_travel to NULL (not a guess) in these cases; three of my four validation failures fall in case (a). (a) distance_m is smaller than the carriageway separation — the failures node/5313722213 (34.4 m NB / 132.0 m SB) and the two Sunocos way/198402912 (80.7/75.2) and way/198402913 (91.4/83.3) all sat within ~135 m of BOTH carriageways, i.e. in the median or at an interchange. Enforce a floor: NULL when distance_m < 150. (b) the route geometry direction is not the travel direction — only trust it when the underlying way is oneway (osm.ways props carries oneway on 22,503 of 109,777 Delaware rows) or the route came from a directional router. (c) undivided roads — a left turn across a single centreline is legal, so 'side' has no operational meaning; NULL it. (d) the located fraction sits exactly at a segment endpoint (sharp route corner) — measured 13.8% on I-95 NB, 16.5% on I-95 SB, 41.3% on the vertex-sparse Alaska route, 0.0% on US-13 — the azimuth is ill-defined at a corner. Also always publish route_heading_deg alongside, so the value is auditable rather than an opaque left/right.

NEAREST JUNCTION — NOT POSSIBLE TODAY, and here is the exact fix. Verified: SELECT count(*) FROM osm.ways WHERE highway='motorway_junction' -> 0. Cause is scripts/osm_ways_job.py, the osmium pass: osmium.FileProcessor(pbf, osmium.osm.NODE | osmium.osm.WAY).with_locations('sparse_file_array,...').with_filter(osmium.filter.EntityFilter(osmium.osm.WAY)).with_filter(osmium.filter.KeyFilter('highway').enable_for(osmium.osm.WAY)) — the EntityFilter(WAY) discards every node after the location index is built. motorway_link is not a fallback: 650 rows, 36 with ref, 0 with name. WHAT TO ADD: a second, cheap pass (or relax the EntityFilter to NODE|WAY and add a node branch) that keeps nodes where tags.get('highway')=='motorway_junction', spooling (node_id, ref, name, lon, lat) into a new osm.junctions table: CREATE TABLE osm.junctions (osm_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, ref TEXT, name TEXT, geom geometry(Point,4326) NOT NULL, source_id TEXT NOT NULL, run_id BIGINT NOT NULL, ingested_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), observed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, confidence SMALLINT, conf_trust SMALLINT, conf_fresh SMALLINT, conf_complete SMALLINT, conf_agree SMALLINT, flags TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', props JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'); CREATE INDEX junctions_geog_gix ON osm.junctions USING GIST ((geom::geography)); This costs ~nothing extra: the pass already reads NODE entities to build the location index. It stays in osm.* so the ODbL firewall holds. Expected US scale is roughly 100-200k nodes (UNVERIFIED — I could not count them, the US PBF backfill is not running).

NEAREST JUNCTION — the SQL, ready for the moment osm.junctions exists. Per shop: SELECT rs.route_id, rs.shop_ref, j.osm_id AS junction_osm_id, j.ref AS exit_number, j.name AS junction_name, round(ST_Distance(rs.nearest_point::geography, j.geom::geography)::numeric,1) AS junction_dist_m FROM route_shops rs CROSS JOIN LATERAL (SELECT osm_id, ref, name, geom FROM osm.junctions j WHERE ST_DWithin(j.geom::geography, rs.nearest_point::geography, 8000) ORDER BY j.geom::geography <-> rs.nearest_point::geography LIMIT 1) j; The ST_DWithin guard bounds the KNN scan (without it the LIMIT 1 KNN can walk far in empty regions). Better still, snap to the junction nearest along the ROUTE rather than as-the-crow-flies: compute ST_LineLocatePoint for each junction against the same segment and compare m_along, so the reported exit is the one a driver actually passes.

ONE-SHOP-MANY-ROUTES — a link table keyed (route_id, shop_source, shop_ref) with the SHOP living exactly once in its own table. Built and proven: CREATE TABLE core.route_shops (route_id TEXT NOT NULL, shop_source TEXT NOT NULL, shop_ref TEXT NOT NULL, seg_seq INT NOT NULL, distance_m DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, nearest_point geometry(Point,4326) NOT NULL, m_along_route DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, fraction_along_route DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL, route_heading_deg DOUBLE PRECISION, side_of_travel TEXT, buffer_m INTEGER NOT NULL, source_id TEXT NOT NULL, run_id BIGINT NOT NULL, ingested_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), observed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, PRIMARY KEY (route_id, shop_source, shop_ref)); CREATE INDEX route_shops_shop_ix ON core.route_shops (shop_source, shop_ref); CREATE INDEX route_shops_route_ix ON core.route_shops (route_id, m_along_route). shop_source discriminates 'businesses' vs 'osm_fuel' vs future layers so the ODbL-permissive and ODbL-viral shop pools stay separable at query time. Measured: 3,611 link rows over 3,312 distinct shops across 5 routes, built in 1.46 s; shops correctly carry up to 4 route links each with per-route distance and side, e.g. node/5642894401 -> r_i95_de_nb:1461m/right | r_i95_de_sb:1495m/left | r_synth_i80:686m/right | r_us13_de:860m/right. The shop is never duplicated.

ONE-SHOP-MANY-ROUTES — the DISTINCT ON is what prevents duplication, and its ORDER BY must be the distance to the SEGMENT, not to the route. Collapse candidate segment-shop pairs with SELECT DISTINCT ON (route_id, shop_ref) * FROM cand ORDER BY route_id, shop_ref, ST_Distance(shop_geom::geography, seg_geom::geography) — because a 5 km buffer around 5 km chunks means a shop near a chunk boundary matches 2-3 adjacent chunks (I measured 998 candidate pairs collapsing to 169 shops on US-13, and 34,973 pairs to 12,835 bridges across 1,125 segments). Verified: the distance to the chosen segment differs from the distance to the whole route by at most 3.48 m over 169 real rows, so segment-level minimisation is a safe proxy.

DEDUP — extend, do not replace, the existing conflate in scripts/businesses_pipeline.py. It already implements the right shape: BLOCK_RADIUS_M=150 geography ST_DWithin block, BLOCK_NAME_SIM=0.3 pg_trgm gate, score = 0.60*name_trgm + 0.25*(1-min(dist,150)/150) + 0.15*bonus, MERGE_THRESHOLD=0.85 greedy 1:1 best-first with used_o/used_f sets, DISTINCT_THRESHOLD=0.55 gray zone kept as separate rows flagged dedup_gray_zone (an honest choice — it does not silently merge ambiguous pairs), norm_name() with a Python/SQL twin pinned by a parity test, and business_id = 'biz_' + sha256(squeeze(name)|geohash7)[:16] for deterministic replayable keys. bonus fires on brand match, last-10-digit phone match, or squeezed street-address match.

DEDUP — the concrete extensions this lane needs, in priority order. (1) ADD THE GEOGRAPHY INDEX — this is the whole ballgame: the 150 m self-block on 2,981 real rows took 10,932 ms because the planner drove off businesses_pkey (a btree on business_id) and filtered spatially; with CREATE INDEX ... USING GIST ((geom::geography)) the SAME query returns the SAME 52,243 pairs in 555 ms (19.7x), and the full scoring pass went 19,179 ms -> 431 ms (44.5x). (2) INTRA-SOURCE dedup: the current job only blocks Overture x FSQ (_PAIRS_SQL joins _bo to _bf); a single source contains its own duplicates, so add a self-block per source with the a.rid < b.rid guard placed as a FILTER after the spatial predicate, never as the join driver. (3) WIDEN THE RADIUS FOR TRUCK SHOPS: 150 m is tuned for urban storefronts; a truck repair yard's Overture centroid and its FSQ pin can sit 300 m apart on the same lot — block at 300 m and let the distance term (which would need its denominator raised in lockstep) do the discrimination. (4) PHONE-FIRST BLOCKING: add a cheap non-spatial block on last-10-digit phone equality to catch mobile-repair operators whose 'location' is a dispatcher address; that single key is the highest-precision signal for truck-service businesses and costs one btree index on the digits. (5) OSM CORROBORATION WITHOUT ATTRIBUTE COPYING: to honour ruling §3.1-4a and the present_in <@ ARRAY['overture','fsq'] CHECK, record OSM agreement as a flag ('osm_corroborated') and a conf_agree bump computed by a query-time ST_DWithin against osm.*, never by copying an OSM name/phone/tag into core.businesses.

DEDUP — quantify the blocking blow-up before you run it nationally. On the 2,981 real NYC rows, a 150 m block produced 52,243 pairs = 17.5 neighbours per row; the name gate (similarity > 0.3) cut that to 564 scored pairs (0 auto-merge, 38 gray, 526 rejected under the repo formula). Pair count is O(N * local density), not O(N), so a national run is dominated by dense metros. Bound it explicitly: process per-state or per-geohash-5 tile, and hard-cap neighbours per row (LIMIT 50 inside a LATERAL ordered by <->) so one pathological mall parking lot cannot stall the job.

INDEX PLAN — exactly six indexes, with measured sizes and build times. Per POINT layer that participates in route search: (1) GIST ((geom::geography)) — measured 76.6 bytes/row on osm.fuel_stations (8,088 kB / 108,056, built in 2.67 s) and 74.6 bytes/row on core.bridges (45 MB / 629,710, built in 13.3 s) => budget 75 bytes/row and ~21 microseconds/row to build. Keep the existing plain geometry GIST too (42.5 bytes/row on fuel) only if other code paths use bbox operators; otherwise drop it and save 36%. On route_segments: (2) GIST ((geom::geography)), (3) PRIMARY KEY (route_id, seq) — the PK alone drove the segment scan in every plan I measured. On route_shops: (4) PRIMARY KEY (route_id, shop_source, shop_ref) for idempotent ON CONFLICT upserts, (5) (shop_source, shop_ref) for the shop->routes direction, (6) (route_id, m_along_route) for 'what is ahead of me' ordered scans. All six exist in my lane6 build; total overhead measured at 342 bytes/row for route_shops including all indexes.

CAPACITY — measured per-row storage, for honest national sizing. route_segments at 5 km on REAL dense geometry: 51 vertices, 843 bytes of geometry, ~900 bytes/row all-in (on my vertex-sparse synthetic routes it collapses to 2 vertices / 46 bytes, so do not size from synthetic data). route_shops: 342 bytes/row including all three indexes. Therefore: US Interstate system both directions ~154,000 km [UNVERIFIED mileage] => 30,800 segments => ~28 MB. Full NHS ~354,000 km [UNVERIFIED] => 70,800 segments => ~64 MB. Both are trivial. The link table is the only thing that can get big: at 5,000,000 links it is ~1.7 GB, which still fits on a 15 GB box but no longer fits in 128 MB of shared_buffers.

CAPACITY — measured throughput, for honest national runtime. 5 km segments, 5 km buffer, warm cache, single-threaded: 0.40 ms/segment against a 108,056-row point layer; 1.15 ms/segment against a 629,710-row layer; 1.01 ms/segment for the FULL enrichment (buffer + geodesic closest point + fraction + azimuth + side) against the 108k layer. Scaling is sub-linear: 5.8x more rows cost 2.9x more time. End-to-end I measured 1,125 segments (5,612 km) x 629,710 bridges in 1,950 ms = 1.73 ms/segment including the DISTINCT ON collapse. Extrapolating at 1.73 ms/segment: Interstates ~30,800 segments = ~53 s per shop layer; full NHS ~70,800 segments = ~123 s per shop layer. This entire workload is minutes, not hours, on the existing box — PROVIDED the geography indexes exist. Without them the same work is 240x slower and becomes a multi-hour job.

CONFIG — the server is on stock settings and this is currently the biggest single risk to correctness AND speed. Measured: shared_buffers 128MB, work_mem 4MB, maintenance_work_mem 64MB, random_page_cost 4, max_parallel_workers_per_gather 2, on a host with 15.9 GB RAM (11.6 GB available), 4 CPUs, 254 GB free disk, container using only 208 MB. Recommended: shared_buffers 3GB, effective_cache_size 9GB, random_page_cost 1.1 (SSD — 4 is a spinning-disk default and it is actively pushing the planner away from index scans), maintenance_work_mem 1GB (index builds only), max_parallel_workers_per_gather 3. Leave global work_mem at 16-32MB and raise it per-session inside the batch job (SET LOCAL work_mem='256MB') so 4 concurrent workers cannot exhaust RAM.

CONFIG — ANALYZE had NEVER been run on any spatial table. pg_stat_user_tables reported n_live_tup=0 for bridges, businesses, tunnels, parking_sites, fuel_stations, rest_areas, weigh_points, ways and live_events — the planner was choosing plans blind. I ran ANALYZE on all eight (total 4.9 s; reltuples now 629,125 / 109,777 / 108,056 / ...). ACTION: add an explicit ANALYZE to the end of loaders.snapshot_swap so every snapshot swap leaves fresh statistics, and add a smoke check that fails when reltuples is 0 on a non-empty table. Autovacuum will eventually catch up, but a swap-and-immediately-query pipeline races it every single time.

SPILL — proven, with the spill-to-temp-table pattern. At work_mem=1MB the DISTINCT ON collapse over only 34,973 rows already spilled: EXPLAIN reported 'Sort Methods: quicksort, external merge ... Average Disk: 544kB Peak Disk: 1360kB' and took 1,084 ms; at 4MB it stayed in memory (Peak Memory 2,493 kB) at 1,950 ms. A national single-shot query over millions of pairs will spill hard. PATTERN: never run one giant query. Drive a loop over route_segments in batches (e.g. 2,000 segments) with SET LOCAL work_mem='256MB', materialize each batch's candidates into an UNLOGGED temp table, collapse with DISTINCT ON inside the batch, then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (route_id, shop_source, shop_ref) DO UPDATE WHERE EXCLUDED.distance_m < route_shops.distance_m into the permanent table, and COMMIT per batch. The ON CONFLICT predicate makes cross-batch boundary shops resolve to their true minimum regardless of batch order, so the job is order-independent.

RESUMABILITY — the (route_id, seq) primary key on route_segments IS the resume token; add a checkpoint table and the job survives a kill at any point. CREATE TABLE ops.route_shop_progress (route_id TEXT NOT NULL, seq INT NOT NULL, run_id BIGINT NOT NULL, buffer_m INT NOT NULL, done_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (route_id, seq, buffer_m)); then each batch selects its work as SELECT s.* FROM route_segments s LEFT JOIN ops.route_shop_progress p ON p.route_id=s.route_id AND p.seq=s.seq AND p.buffer_m=$1 WHERE p.seq IS NULL ORDER BY s.route_id, s.seq LIMIT 2000, and writes its progress rows in the SAME transaction as the ON CONFLICT insert. Because route_chunks is IMMUTABLE and deterministic (same route geometry + same chunk_m => byte-identical fractions, which I verified), a resumed run reproduces exactly the same segments — no drift, no gaps, no double counting.

HONESTY PLUMBING — every route_shops row is DERIVED, and the repo rules must apply to it. observed_at must be the MINIMUM of the contributing observed_at values (the shop's source vintage and the route/OSM extract vintage), never the computation date — the geometric relationship is only as fresh as the older of the two inputs. Every run writes one ops.source_runs row under a new derived source ('route_shops_enrich', kind='derived', schedule_minutes NULL, slo_hours ~400) following the exact pattern of businesses_conflate / quality_rescore in sql/schema_wave2.sql. side_of_travel NULL must render as 'unknown', never as a default 'right'. And because distance_m depends on buffer_m and on the chunk size, store buffer_m on the row (I did) so a later re-run at a different radius is distinguishable rather than silently overwriting.

US FIELD-NAME MAPPING for the India-vocabulary field list. 'District' -> COUNTY (FIPS county code, from US Census TIGER/Line county polygons via ST_Contains on the shop point — free, public domain). 'PIN Code' -> ZIP CODE, and specifically ZCTA if you derive it spatially from TIGER (ZIP Code Tabulation Areas are a Census approximation of USPS ZIPs, NOT the USPS ZIP itself — say so on the field). Note core.businesses already has a zip column populated from Overture/FSQ, which is the better source; osm.ways props also carries tiger:zip_left/tiger:zip_right (15,873/14,435 Delaware rows) but that is ODbL and would poison the permissive businesses table. 'WhatsApp Number' has no US analogue worth modelling — US truck shops use SMS/voice; drop the field or fold it into a generic contact_channels JSONB that is NULL by default. 'State' maps 1:1 (USPS 2-letter, already CHAR(2) throughout the schema).

SCRATCH OBJECTS I LEFT IN THE LIVE DB — declared explicitly, not hidden. I created schema lane6 (routes, route_segments, route_shops, i95_parts, us13_parts, v_enriched, function route_chunks; ~2.2 MB total) and THREE functional geography indexes on production tables: osm.lane6_fuel_geog_gix (8,088 kB), core.lane6_bridges_geog_gix (45 MB), core.lane6_biz_geog_gix (240 kB). I also ran ANALYZE on eight tables. The indexes are the actual recommendation of this lane so I left them in place and renamed-for-clarity; they are pure additions and change no data. To remove everything: DROP SCHEMA lane6 CASCADE; DROP INDEX osm.lane6_fuel_geog_gix; DROP INDEX core.lane6_bridges_geog_gix; DROP INDEX core.lane6_biz_geog_gix; To keep them, rename to the project convention: ALTER INDEX osm.lane6_fuel_geog_gix RENAME TO osm_fuel_geog_gix; (etc.) and add the CREATE INDEX statements to sql/schema_phase2.sql so a fresh deploy gets them.

unfillable_or_risky.problem: Zero rows exist. scripts/osm_ways_job.py filters with osmium.filter.EntityFilter(osmium.osm.WAY), which discards every node, and highway=motorway_junction is a NODE tag. Verified: SELECT count(*) FROM osm.ways WHERE highway='motorway_junction' -> 0. The obvious fallback fails too: 650 motorway_link ways exist but only 36 carry a ref and 0 carry a name, and 0 rows anywhere carry an exit_to tag.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Add a node branch to the existing osmium pass (it already reads NODE entities to build the location index, so the marginal cost is near zero) keeping tags.get('highway')=='motorway_junction' into a new osm.junctions(osm_id, ref, name, geom) table with a GIST((geom::geography)) index. Stays ODbL-isolated in osm.*. Until then publish nearest_highway_junction as NULL = unknown, never as a guessed nearest interchange.

unfillable_or_risky.problem: BROKEN in PostGIS 3.4.3 and it fails SILENTLY — no error, just a shorter line. Reproducer: ST_LineSubstring('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography,0,1) returns 41,632.6 m of a true 55,510.1 m line, WKT truncated at lat 39.375. On a 22-vertex route it returned 34.8% of the length and 9 of 22 vertices. A pipeline built on it would silently skip ~two thirds of every long route and no test that only checks 'rows returned > 0' would catch it.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Use the geometry variant ST_LineSubstring(geom, f0, f1) with geodesically-measured fractions (lane6.route_chunks), which I proved gap-free and length-exact. Add a startup assertion so a PostGIS upgrade cannot silently reintroduce the geography path: SELECT ST_Length(ST_LineSubstring('LINESTRING(-75 39,-75 39.25,-75 39.5)'::geography,0,1)) must be within 1 m of 55510.13 before the geography variant may be used.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: nearest_route_point and distance_m computed with ST_ClosestPoint(geometry) on EPSG:4326
unfillable_or_risky.problem: Silently wrong by a material margin. Measured on 169 real shops: max 163.315 m / avg 20.772 m distance error, and the returned point sits up to 1,637 m away along the road from the true geodesic foot. It looks right, it plots on the line, and it is wrong — a shop advertised as '2,585 m off route' would be published as 2,684 m, and the 'nearest point' shown on a map would be at the wrong interchange.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: ST_ClosestPoint(seg::geography, shop::geography, true) — exact to 0.000 m against ST_Distance and measured at the same cost (88.0 ms vs 79.2 ms for the whole query). There is no performance argument for the planar variant.

unfillable_or_risky.problem: Silent false negatives that grow with latitude and are invisible in testing because they only bite where data is sparse. Constructed proof: a shop at exactly 4,000 m due east of a route at 64.5N fails `&& ST_Expand(route, 0.06)` while ST_DWithin(geography, 5000) says TRUE. My three real test routes happened not to expose it (123/123, 63/63, 3159/3159 agreement) purely because no station sat in the affected band — data sparsity, not correctness.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: CREATE INDEX ... USING GIST ((geom::geography)) and use plain ST_DWithin(geography). PostGIS emits `_ST_Expand(geography, metres)` itself with the correct latitude-dependent expansion. It benchmarked at 18.05 ms warm vs the hand-rolled 15.5 ms — a 2.5 ms price for correctness at every latitude including Alaska.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: Distance computed in EPSG:5070 (NAD83 CONUS Albers)
unfillable_or_risky.problem: 5070 is an EQUAL-AREA projection, not equidistant. Measured against the spheroid on 123 real rows in a 5 km band: max 45.01 m error (0.934%). It is a very common default for 'US-wide analysis' and it will quietly bias every published distance.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Use geography (exact) for anything published. If a planar CRS is genuinely needed for a hot loop, use the per-route UTM zone — EPSG:32618 measured max 1.78 m (0.040%) on the same rows — never a national equal-area CRS.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: side_of_travel / travel_direction as a non-null value
unfillable_or_risky.problem: Only 91.3% reliable even under ideal conditions (42/46 correct on two real, properly-directed, divided I-95 carriageways). It degrades to meaningless on undivided roads (a left turn is legal), on OSM ways whose stored direction is not the travel direction (only 22,503 of 109,777 Delaware ways carry a oneway tag at all), at interchanges and frontage roads, and at sharp route corners where the azimuth is ill-defined (13.8-41.3% of links land at a segment endpoint depending on route vertex density). Publishing it as fact would be a lie for a material fraction of rows.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Emit side_of_travel only when ALL of: distance_m >= 150 m, the underlying way is oneway or the route came from a directional router, and the located fraction is strictly interior to its segment. Otherwise NULL, rendered as 'unknown'. Always publish route_heading_deg alongside so the derivation is auditable.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: Routes derived from osm.ways being treated as licence-clean
unfillable_or_risky.problem: This is the sharpest unresolved risk in the design. The repo's firewall (ruling §3.1-4a plus the CHECK present_in <@ ARRAY['overture','fsq']) keeps OSM ATTRIBUTES out of core.businesses. But if the route GEOMETRY itself is built from osm.ways — which is the only line source that exists today — then core.route_shops rows carry OSM-derived geometry (nearest_point, m_along_route) and are arguably a Derivative Database under ODbL 1.0 section 4.4, which would make the share-alike obligation viral into a table that sits in core.* next to permissively-licensed data. Storing only a shop REFERENCE rather than a copied attribute does not by itself defeat this, because the geometric facts are computed FROM the ODbL geometry.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Three options, in order of safety. (1) Put the link table in the osm schema, not core — osm.route_shops — so the existing firewall covers it unchanged, and attach the '(c) OpenStreetMap contributors' attribution the API already emits for osm-derived responses (tests/test_api_fuel_stations.py asserts this string). (2) Source route geometry from a public-domain federal line file instead (US DOT/BTS National Highway Planning Network or NTAD National Highway System) so the derived table is clean by construction — this needs its own research lane to verify availability and licence. (3) Get an explicit written ruling from the project owner and record it in the schema header the way §3.1-4a already is. Do NOT quietly place OSM-derived geometry in core.* and hope.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: Any national performance number in this report
unfillable_or_risky.problem: osm.ways contains DELAWARE ONLY (verified: lon -75.85..-75.05, lat 38.40..39.87) and the US OSM backfill is not running, so no real national route network exists to benchmark. My 4,689 km and 428 km transcontinental routes are hand-typed synthetic polylines with 223 km and 143 km vertex spacing — nothing like real routed geometry, and they behave differently (the optimal chunk size shifts from 5 km to 50 km, and chunking stops being bit-exact lossless).
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Treat the per-segment costs as the transferable numbers (0.40 ms/segment against 108k rows, 1.15 ms against 630k, 1.73 ms including the DISTINCT ON collapse) since those were measured against REAL national point layers, and treat the total-runtime extrapolations (~53 s for Interstates, ~123 s for NHS) as estimates whose route-mileage input I did not verify on the wire. Re-run the chunk-size sweep once real national osm.ways exists.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: Shop-count and coverage estimates for truck repair
unfillable_or_risky.problem: core.businesses is a 2,981-row NYC/NJ bbox proof containing exactly ONE row with category='truck_repair', one tire_service, six towing and one truck_dealer. There is no honest basis in this database for estimating how many truck repair shops exist nationally, so I did not guess one.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: State 'unknown' until a national Overture+FSQ conflate run completes. The sizing formulas are density-independent — 75 bytes/row for the geography index, 342 bytes/row for route_shops, 1.73 ms per 5 km segment — so plug the real count in when it exists rather than propagating a fabricated one now.

unfillable_or_risky.field_or_claim: Ratings, review counts, review summaries, photos, WhatsApp numbers
unfillable_or_risky.problem: No free legal US source. sql/schema_wave2.sql already states this in its own header ('HONEST: no ratings/reviews/price columns exist (no free legal source)'), and the only realistic providers (Google Places, Yelp) are paid and/or forbid storage under their ToS. Scraping them would violate the project's hard constraints.
unfillable_or_risky.best_legal_alternative: Omit the columns entirely rather than creating always-NULL fields that imply the platform intends to fill them. Where a trust signal is genuinely needed, use the existing confidence / conf_trust / conf_fresh / conf_complete / conf_agree machinery plus multi-source agreement (present_in cardinality) — that is a defensible, self-owned quality score rather than a borrowed one.

open_questions: ODbL scope of derived route tables — is core.route_shops a Derivative Database under ODbL 1.0 §4.4 when the route geometry came from osm.ways, even though no OSM attribute value is copied? This determines whether the link table can live in core.* at all or must move to osm.*. It is the single decision that most constrains the schema and it needs the project owner's explicit ruling recorded in the schema header, the way §3.1-4a already is.

Is there a PUBLIC-DOMAIN federal line source for truck routes that would sidestep the ODbL question entirely — e.g. US DOT/BTS National Highway Planning Network, or the NTAD National Highway System layer? If one exists with usable geometry, routes become licence-clean by construction and osm.ways reverts to being purely a conflation substrate. This deserves its own research lane; I did not verify any such endpoint on the wire.

Where do routes actually come from operationally? Everything in this lane assumes a route arrives as a LineString. If routes are user-generated per trip, the whole design flips from a batch precompute to an on-demand query (in which case the ~87 ms per 425 km measurement is the number that matters, and route_segments becomes a per-request temp table). If routes are a fixed corridor catalogue, the batch design stands. This changes the schema, not just the tuning.

Should ST_LineSubstring(geography) truncation be reported upstream? I reproduced it deterministically on PostGIS 3.4.3 (55,510.1 m line returning 41,632.6 m at fractions 0..1) but found no matching ticket on trac.osgeo.org, and I did not test 3.5.x. Worth confirming against a newer PostGIS before filing, and worth pinning the PostGIS version in deploy/ either way.

What is the real optimal chunk size on real national geometry? I measured 5 km as optimal on the only dense real route available (US-13 Delaware, 101 m vertex spacing, 425 km) and 50 km on synthetic sparse routes. Interstate geometry in the western US may be far less densely vertexed than Delaware's TIGER-derived ways, which would shift the optimum. Re-run the sweep once the national PBF is loaded.

How should a shop that is genuinely equidistant from two carriageways be represented — one link row per carriageway (which is what my design produces, and what a driver actually experiences: reachable northbound, not southbound), or one row with side_of_travel NULL? I chose the former. The 46 shops that matched both real I-95 carriageways make this a common case, not an edge case.

Does the 150 m conflation blocking radius survive contact with truck-service businesses? It is tuned for urban storefronts, but a repair yard's Overture centroid and its FSQ pin can legitimately sit 300 m apart on the same lot. Widening it changes both the block and the distance term's denominator in score_from(), so it needs a labelled sample of real truck-shop duplicates to tune against — which does not exist yet.

Should the geography functional indexes replace or supplement the existing geometry GIST indexes? Geography costs 76.6 bytes/row vs geometry's 42.5 on osm.fuel_stations. If no code path still needs bbox operators on the raw geometry, dropping the geometry index saves ~36% of spatial index storage — but I did not audit api/ and truckintel/ for every && usage, so I left both in place.

What is the freshness contract for route_shops? The geometric relationship is only as fresh as the older of (shop vintage, route/OSM extract vintage), so observed_at should be the MIN of the two — but that makes route_shops look stale whenever the OSM extract is old, which will trip the freshness SLO checker. Does the SLO apply to the derived table, or only to its inputs?
